segments.text: A mother gave her daughter to a man dying on a stake.
For a thousand gold coins, he wanted a son after his death.
I'm Mohan Kaka, your storyteller tonight.
And this is the corpse's seventh story.
Last tale's riddle, who was truly generous?
Vikram answered, the thief.
A husband cannot keep a wife whose heart is elsewhere.
The friend no longer wanted another man's wife,
but a thief let go of bride and all her gold.
The corpse flew back, Vikram touched it again, and it began a new story.
When the Navatis father died, his relatives seized everything.
She fled with her mother by night.
Outside town, her mother walked into something in the dark.
A man on a stake, still alive.
He groaned, who rubbed salt into my wounds?
The moon rose.
He saw the Navati and said, a thousand gold coins.
Make her my wife.
Her mother laughed.
What do you want with her?
No son, no peace after death.
Let her have a son by any man.
He will be mine.
For the gold, her mother agreed,
and poured the wedding water on his hand.
He told them where his gold lay, then he died.
They carried the thief's gold to a far city.
From her roof, the Navati saw a poor young scholar.
She remembered the thief's order.
He named his price, 500 gold coins.
One night, the thief's gold paid him.
By morning, he was gone.
She had a son.
A dream told her, leave him at the king's gate with the thief's gold.
The old king had no son.
He dreamed of a child at his gate.
A dawn, a baby on a heap of gold.
He raised him as his own, and the boy became king.
The old king died.
His son walked to the holy well of Gaia.
He held out the offering for his father.
The water moved, his rose out the well.
One held an iron spike, a thief's hand.
One held a book, a scholar's hand.
One wore a ring, a king's hand.
Even the priests did not know.
Three hands, one son, one offering.
King, into whose hand should it go?
Stay silent and your head splits.
So whose son is he?
The thief who gave him a name?
The man who gave him blood?
Or the king who gave him a life?
